entry.content:
Author's note: Originally written September 2026. Posting was delayed due to Publii posting issues.

For the past 9 months, I've been grinding away at Cisco Network Academy's three part CCNA course. Why? Because I saw a graphic showing that the CCNA, plus two certificates I already had, the CompTIAA Network+ and Security+, were great qualifiers for a cybersecurity network engineer.

Having finally completed that grueling marathon, I'll talk about what I liked, didn't like, and some tips for prospective students.

Table of Contents

  • What I liked
    • User Driven Pacing
    • IOS Command Practice
    • Packet Tracer Exercises
    • Unlimited Retries
  • What I Didn't Like
    • Academic Prose
    • Gaps in Interactivity
    • Not Being Able to Copy Text
    • Quiz/Exam Errors
    • Packet Tracer Exam Timers
    • The Course Survey
  • Tips for Prospective Students
    • Pace Yourself
    • Download the Practice Exams
    • Do the Final Twice
    • Write Down the IOS Commands
  • Takeaways

What I liked

User Driven Pacing

One of the greatest benefits of online only/online primary education schemes is the self-paced nature. You can go as fast or slow as you want/need, instead of being held prisoner by how fast your teacher and/or fellow students can get through the material.

Now, there's some tips I'll get into later about this, but overall, I'd say it's a positive.

Cisco Network Academy breaks up the CCNA into three courses. I wound up completing each course in 2.5 to 3 months, with the majority of that time spending 2-3 days per week on the course material. I believe it's easily possible to beat my pace, depending on your circumstances.

IOS Command Practice

Another positive is that Network Academy actually has a decent amount of interactivity. One area where that is greatly appreciated is Cisco IOS command practice.

Cisco IOS is a command line interface operating system for Cisco routers and switches. There are a multitude of commands you'll be exposed to throughout each course, and memorizing them definitely helps with the Packet Tracer exercises. One thing that definitely helps with memorization is using the commands, which doesn't require the full Packet Tracer experience.

Syntax Checker is an interactive CLI simulator where you're given a task related to recent lessons. Each task is broken down into multiple steps that require Cisco IOS commands to execute some Cisco device configuration. Crucially, it allows you to reveal what a specific command is, or even the entire set of commands. That means you're never going to be trapped in an exercise, unable to complete it.

Syntax Checker has a few drawbacks though:

  1. The instructions are contained within the same window as your inputs, so if you get a streak of typos, you're going to have to start scrolling.
  2. Syntax Checker will only accept complete commands and pre-approved abbreviations. Everything else counts as incorrect input.

Item number 2 on that list is the most frustrating. The problem with CLI is that the longer and more complex your command strings are, the more probable it is that you're going to typo somewhere. Cisco IOS itself actually allows you to use abbreviated versions of the commands without an issue, but Syntax Checker doesn't.

At most, Syntax Checker will allow abbreviations for interfaces. For example, instead of gigabyteethernet 0/0/0, you get told to use g0/0/0. This does save you some time and typos, but you'll probably stumble a few times on new commands.

My personal recommendation is getting 3 to 5 clean passes on Syntax Checker before moving on. That should make it easier to deal with the next item on the list.

Packet Tracer Exercises

Packet Tracer is a free Cisco network simulation program, with the caveat that it requires a Cisco account. Since you're already doing Network Academy, you have an account, which mitigates that headache. Packet Tracer also has a periodic account check, which handles itself automatically.

One of the best things about Cisco Network Academy is that you download all the exercises and their instructions, allowing you to keep them forever. This means you can take as much time as you want/need to go through each one, and even return to them years down the line for a refresher.

(Downloading the PDF is unnecessary, because the Packet Tracer exercise has the instructions built in. Viewing the PDF, however, is necessary, as part of the Network Academy progress tracking.)

The exercises also incorporate a progress checker, allowing you to spot check your own work to a degree. It won't give you exact errors, but it'll visibly show if you've gotten something correct or not.

The most likely thing to trip you up on these exercises, besides forgetting/typo-ing commands, is subnetting. Many of the exercises will demand you use the network address of Y subnet of an X subnetted network, and it's really easy to get tripped up here.

The next most likely thing to trip you up is removing cables in physical mode without resetting the whole exercise. Cisco's Packet Tracer tutorials are pretty terrible, so it's easy to get far along without knowing how to do this. The easiest way I've found is to inspect the front/rear of the switch/router that has a cable connected, click the cable in the interface, then click the pegboard filled with cables.

Thankfully, there's a lot of Packet Tracer exercise tutorial videos to help you figure out where you went wrong and learn how to do things right.

Unlimited Retries

One of the most miserable elements of gaining certificates is that they require a hefty time and/or money investment, and all of that can end in failure.

So it's actually a relief that Cisco Network Academy gives you unlimited tries on the online portions.

This shifts the quizzes and exams from "all or nothing, failure is not an option" to a more casual "you think you're up to the challenge?" type engagement. You can bullrush right into them just to see how well you'd do or to discover what your blindspots are. You can take the time to study before each one. All strategies are valid, and you're not penalized for your choice. The only cost is time.

This includes the practice exams, both the multiple choice exam and the Packet Tracer exam. (There are in fact multiple practice Packet Tracer exams, and they're almost always harder than the actual final PT exam.)

So feel free to take as many shots as you want/need at a challenging quiz/exam!

What I Didn't Like

Academic Prose

If you've read any textbooks, you know what I'm talking about.

Academic prose is an exhausting thing to read, because it's just slightly too verbose and tends to bury the actually useful information in filler. This is especially miserable for people who take handwritten notes like me, because I have to spend time reading the text, figuring out what's actually important, looping back to make sure I don't miss something, and then proceeding.

Many sections are not that bad, but all it takes is one module where it's mostly academic prose for your momentum to nose dive.

Even worse, some quiz/exam answers are buried in the academic prose, making getting through the stuff more annoying.

November 2026 update: Continuing with more Cisco NetAcademy has convinced me that a better workflow is reading the prose, then using browser inspection or other tools to feed the text to an LLM. This can make a distilled version that's more friendly to your preferred note format.

Gaps in Interactivity

No course can be 100% hands on. Everything requires some amount of theory and fact-based learning. But two of Network Academy's CCNA courses definitely feel like they can be better balanced.

The first CCNA course was pretty well balanced, peppering plenty of Syntax Checker and Packet Tracer exercises throughout its length. You never got multiple back-to-back sections of nothing but academic prose, which helped maintain interest and momentum.

The other two courses feel like very brief peaks of interactivity, separated by massive valleys of academic prose. This makes it hard to retain IOS skills and knowledge, at least without a practice regimen. For example, there was what felt like a month long gap between Cisco IOS exercises, and it absolutely made reengaging with IOS a miserable experience.

It's especially annoying because many of the more complex Cisco IOS settings/configurations get way less exercises than the basics. The gaps IOS or even Syntax Checker exercises makes it harder to retain and build on that knowledge. While watching tutorial videos on YouTube can help, it'd be better to not have the problem in the first place.

Not Being Able to Copy Text

Cisco Network Academy doesn't let you copy the text of its course material.

On one hand, understandable, because they presumably spent money within the last decade to update the material.

On the other hand, so much of its is fluffed up academic prose that it'd be nice to highlight that text, copy it, paste in a word processor, and rewrite it into something readable.

And yes, that's basically what I do when I make my handwritten notes. But again, it's an annoying and time consuming process that sucks the momentum out of the experience. Whereas copying the text as soon as it loads, pasting it, and editing it as a I read it is a much faster process.

Also, being able to copy the text would hopefully mean being able to copy the many text charts in the material. I wound up making almost 80 screen captures of charts and infographics for the third course alone. I also can't make a digital version of my notes unless I go through a time consuming OCR process. If I'd been able to copy the notes from the site, I could've easily made myself an eBook, put on my phone and other devices, and referenced it whenever I wanted.

Quiz/Exam Errors

There's nothing more annoying than taking a quiz or test, answering with what you know the text says is the right answer, and then finding out, nope, it's the wrong answer!

This isn't a particularly specific criticism for Network Academy, since I've seen this in just about every online platform. That said, Network Academy, as far as I can tell, doesn't give users any real way to flag issues with the quizzes/exams.

So you get to have the fun experience of everything you read saying one thing, while the quiz/exam says another!

Packet Tracer Exam Timers

The practice and final exams are timed events, each lasting 75 minutes (one hour, 15 minutes). I have no issues with timed exams.

I do have a problem when the exam timer starts before you even download the Packet Tracer exam file.

Here's what happens when you do one of the Packet Tracer exams (practical/final):

  1. You press a button to bring up the exam page.
  2. You press another button to actually download the Packet Tracer file.
  3. The Packet Tracer file downloads and opens.

The timer starts after step 1, so you lose up to a minute while steps 2 and 3 execute. You can then lose up to another minute if you have to copy and paste the network address chart and instructions into a word processor to make them readable. (Unlike other Packet Tracer files, the exams use the left third of the window for instructions/reference information.)

The stress naturally increases as the time decreases, so losing time while not even being able to engage with the exam feels terrible.

Now, you be going, "Losing a minute to a minute and a half at the start is not a big deal", but remember, this is stacking with however long it takes you to read the instructions, execute tasks, double check the instructions, and recover from mistakes. The ideal situation is having at least 5 minutes to do any last minute checks/fixes before submitting the result.

Oddly, the Packet Tracer exams have an online connection to a server where your progress is auto-saved/submitted. So it should be possible to have the Packet Tracer program on your PC send packet to the server when the file is 90-95% loaded to trigger the timer. Then, when your system opens the Packet Tracer file, you get up to the full 75 minutes, regardless of network conditions.

The Course Survey

I don't have a problem with end of course surveys. I have a problem with bad end of course surveys.

As you can see from my screen capture gallery, you just get 10 multiple or ranked choice questions, with no real ability to submit more detailed feedback. So Cisco has no real way to get information about what it doesn't do well, which means they don't have any chance of improving.

The point of dedicated feedback like this is to provide a pipeline of clear, insightful data to the team maintaining the content. Without a single optional field for freeform text input, there's no actual way to send a direct message to that team that isn't going to have bounce around whatever Cisco's end user facing contact system is.

Tips for Prospective Students

Pace Yourself

The key to a good self-learning experience is knowing how to pace yourself.

For example, I probably could've gotten through the whole thing faster if I'd maintained a 4-5 day a week schedule. And in fact, when I started and when I ended the entire CCNA course process, I did do that. But I could only achieve that pace in the beginning because the first course started with a lot of material I was already familiar with from other courses. And at the end, I was already done with the reading, so I could spend time with the practice exams, rereading all my notes, and then taking the final exams on two separate days.

However, by the time I completed the first section, I was already heading towards a 2 to 3 days of Network Academy per week schedule. Why? Because I was feeling burnt out. Going through the material that fast was tiring, especially when I had two more whole courses to get through.

By taking few days per week to go through the material, I recharged my mental batteries on off-days by doing other things. That helped me get through the particularly boring, academic prose only days.

Is that the way you should do it? Maybe, maybe not. But it's something that's good to think about before you start.

Download the Practice Exams

This is the single best tip to keep you from being bored, while also requiring the least number of Packet Tracer exercises to juggle.

As I pointed out earlier, the Packet Tracer practice exams for each course are almost always harder than the final exam. This is because they cover a lot of the more complicated aspects of Cisco IOS configuration that you tend to lose over during the valleys of academic prose. That makes them ideal for keeping your skills sharp.

There's just one problem: you can't download them from Cisco Network Academy.

Before you get your outrage pony going, you can get the Packet Tracer exercise files. You just have to look elsewhere. My personal recommendation is this YouTube channel, which does Cisco Packet Tracer exercise tutorials. The instruction PDFs and exercise files can be found in the descriptions of the relevant videos.

(Note: The channel's video naming scheme isn't great, so pick the video that's most recent to when you're watching.)

My recommendation is to do them at least once every two weeks during the academic prose only sections of the courses. You could even cycle between different ones each week. That way you keep in practice and give yourself something more interactive to carry you through those less engaging sections.

Do the Final Twice

This isn't saying you shouldn't do your best on the first try. It's reminding you of two things:

  1. You've got unlimited tries.
  2. You'll have a better idea of what you're facing the second time around.

In particular, the Packet Tracer final is going to be a lot easier if you follow these steps:

  1. Copy the network address chart and instructions to a word processor/text document.
  2. Complete your first try.
  3. Reorganize the instructions so things are faster/easier.

Step 3 is, at its core, just making sure you do all the tasks on one type of machine before another. If the instructions are mostly router configuration, getting through that first will make it easier to deal with switches, and vice versa. This especially helps with Packet Tracer finals where you need to unplug and replug multiple console connections, which cut into your time as well.

Keep in mind that everything you do in the Packet Tracer exam counts for only 1 point, and there's no points given for doing things in order.

What about troubleshooting, you say? Well, while there might be some advantage of doing things in the original order and testing as you go, you're on the clock. Being able to go faster, because you're not switching between devices as often, means that you have more time to test and troubleshoot before you submit.

(It's also more realistic, but let's not get into that argument.)

I managed to go from an 85% grade on my first try at the final course Packet Tracer exam to a 96%, just by reorganizing the instructions and looking up the command for a task that never got used in any other exercises. The time I saved setting up devices gave me enough time to realize that I had misread which PC to TFTP copy configuration files to, allowing me to earn 3 points I would've otherwise lost.

Write Down the IOS Commands

Cisco IOS is a case of two extremes. You've got commands that are easy to burn into your mind, like conf t or switch mode access, and then you've got commands where you might have problems remembering the details of, like crypto key gen rsa general-keys mod 1024 or spanning-tree portfast bpduguard.

How can you remember these commands better? Well, do what people have been doing for years: write down all the Cisco IOS commands in a text document on your computer, and pull it up when you need to do exercises.

It's a simple, brute force solution to the memory problem. You get an extra repetition of writing out the command, plus the advantage of adding contextual notes, like what mode and when to use it. And by doing it all in one document, you can optimize the order of the commands when possible, to make remembering and executing the commands faster and easier.

It is probably going to be a decently long document, but considering how often you could/should be engaging with the Packet Tracer exercises, it's well worth it. You can even take it forward with you into a network engineering job and just keep building it up.

Takeaways

User-Driven Pacing

  • Self-paced online learning lets students move as fast or slow as needed without being limited by a teacher or class schedule.
  • Finished each of the three CCNA courses in roughly 2.5 to 3 months, usually spending 2 to 3 days per week on the material.
  • Faster completion is possible depending on the student’s circumstances.

IOS Command Practice

  • Network Academy provides interactive practice that helps students learn Cisco IOS commands without needing a full Packet Tracer environment.
  • Syntax Checker gives step-by-step CLI configuration tasks and allows users to reveal individual commands or the full answer, so students are not permanently stuck.
  • Drawbacks: the instructions and command input share the same window, causing extra scrolling when typos occur; Syntax Checker only accepts complete commands or pre-approved abbreviations.
  • I recommend getting 3 to 5 clean passes on Syntax Checker before moving on.

Packet Tracer Exercises

  • Packet Tracer is a free Cisco network simulator that requires a Cisco account, but Network Academy students already have one.
  • The required Cisco account check is handled automatically.
  • Exercises and instructions can be downloaded and kept permanently, allowing repeated practice and future review.
  • A built-in progress checker shows whether parts are correct, though it does not provide exact error details.
  • External tutorial videos can help students identify mistakes and learn proper Packet Tracer techniques.

Unlimited Retries

  • Unlimited attempts on online quizzes and exams reduce the all-or-nothing pressure of certification testing.
  • Students can rush an assessment to find weak areas or prepare thoroughly before trying; the main cost is time.
  • This applies to both multiple-choice and Packet Tracer practice exams.
  • There are multiple practice Packet Tracer exams, and they are usually harder than the actual final Packet Tracer exam.

Academic Prose

  • Much of the course text is verbose and can bury useful information in filler.
  • This is especially frustrating for note-takers who must read, identify key points, reread to verify, write, and then move on.
  • One weak module can kill momentum.
  • Some quiz or exam answers are hidden in the prose, making the material more annoying to work through.
  • Consider reading the text, then using tools to extract course text and feed it to an LLM to generate a note friendly version.

Gaps in Interactivity

  • No course can be entirely hands-on, but two of the three CCNA courses feel poorly balanced between theory and practice.
  • The first course is well balanced, with frequent Syntax Checker and Packet Tracer activities.
  • The other two courses have short interactive peaks separated by long stretches of academic prose.
  • Long gaps between IOS exercises make it hard to retain and build on commands, especially for complex configurations.
  • More advanced Cisco IOS settings receive fewer exercises than basic commands.
  • YouTube tutorials can help, but better built-in practice would reduce the problem.

Not Being Able to Copy Text

  • The platform does not allow users to copy course text.
  • The restriction is understandable if the material was recently updated, but it is frustrating when the text is wordy.
  • It would be optimal to copy text into a word processor and rewrite it into clearer notes.
  • Copying would also allow copying text-based charts and infographics; I made about 80 screenshots for the third course alone.
  • Without copy access, creating digital notes requires time-consuming OCR or manual re-entry.

Quiz/Exam Errors

  • It's frustrating when a quiz or exam marks an answer wrong even though the course text says that answer is correct.
  • I've seen this on many online platforms, but Network Academy does not provide a useful way to flag quiz or exam errors.

Packet Tracer Exam Timers

  • Packet Tracer practice and final exams are timed at 75 minutes.
  • The timer starts before the student downloads and opens the Packet Tracer exam file, costing up to about one minute.
  • An additional minute may be lost if the student copies the on-screen instructions and network address chart into a word processor to make them readable.
  • The exam instructions occupy the left third of the Packet Tracer window, making them less convenient to read.
  • The lost time stacks on top of reading instructions, completing tasks, double-checking work, and recovering from mistakes.
  • Since the exam file auto-saves to a server, the timer could theoretically start when the file is mostly loaded, giving students the full 75 minutes.

The Course Survey

  • The end-of-course survey is poor because it only has about 10 multiple-choice or ranked-choice questions.
  • It lacks a free-form field, preventing students from giving detailed feedback.
  • Without free-form feedback, Cisco has little direct insight into what the course does poorly and how to improve.

Pace Yourself

  • Self-learning success depends on choosing a sustainable pace.
  • I initially used a 4 to 5 days-per-week pace because the first course covered familiar material, then ended the final course with a similar pace.
  • After the first section, I settled into 2 to 3 days per week to avoid burnout.
  • Off-days helped recharge mental energy and made the boring, prose-heavy sections easier to endure.
  • Students should think about their own pacing before starting, though the author’s approach may not be best for everyone.

Download the Practice Exams

  • Downloading and working through Packet Tracer practice exams is the best way to reduce boredom and maintain hands-on skills.
  • It also minimizes the number of separate Packet Tracer exercises you need to juggle.
  • Practice Packet Tracer exams are usually harder than the final exam because they cover complex IOS configuration topics that fade during long prose sections.
  • The practice exam files are not downloadable directly from Network Academy, but they can be found elsewhere.
  • Do a practice exam at least once every two weeks during prose-only sections, or cycle through different exams weekly.

Do the Final Twice

  • Students should still do their best on the first attempt, but unlimited retries and improved familiarity make a second attempt valuable.
  • For the Packet Tracer final, copy the network address chart and instructions into a text document or word processor.
  • Complete the first attempt, then reorganize the instructions to make the second attempt faster and easier.
  • Key strategy: complete all tasks on one type of device before moving to another, such as finishing router work before switch work.
  • This is especially helpful when the exam requires unplugging and replugging multiple console connections, which wastes time.
  • Every task in the Packet Tracer exam is worth 1 point, and there is no bonus for doing tasks in the original order.
  • Although following the original order can help with testing as you go, reducing device switching gives more time to troubleshoot before submitting.

Write Down the IOS Commands

  • Cisco IOS contains both simple commands that are easy to remember and complex commands that are hard to recall in full.
  • A practical solution is to create a text document listing all Cisco IOS commands you need to learn.
  • Writing the commands adds repetition, and adding notes about mode and usage improves recall.
  • The same document can be carried into a network engineering job and continued to grow.

entry.title: Quick Thoughts: TrueNAS 25.04 Restoring Default Route
entry.summary: This guide provides a clear, step-by-step procedure to restore a missing default route on TrueNAS 25.04 using the native midclt…
entry.content:
This guide provides a clear, step-by-step procedure to restore a missing default route on TrueNAS 25.04 using the native midclt API. You may encounter this issue when adding new interface cards to your TrueNAS server.

This issue can disable your Docker containers and ability to update the OS. Unfortunately, there's no easily accessible documentation on how to fix it, so here's a tutorial on how to do it.

Prerequisites:

  • SSH, web GUI, or text console access to the TrueNAS shell.
  • Root or equivalent privileges.
  • TrueNAS 25.04 with the interface and route APIs available.

Important:

  • Run all commands from the TrueNAS shell.
  • Keep the Web UI open in another window for reference.
  • Do not interrupt or close the session while a transaction is pending.

Table of Contents

  • High-Level Overview
  • Phase 1: Pre-Flight Diagnostics
    • Step 1: Check for pending changes
    • Step 2: Check if the default route would be removed
  • Phase 2: Confirm Current State
    • Step 3: Inspect configuration, interface, and routes
  • Phase 3: Create a Safe Interface Update
    • Step 4: Get current interface configuration
    • Step 5: Apply a temporary description change
  • Phase 4: Inject Gateway and Commit (with Rollback Protection)
    • Step 6: Capture the configured gateway
    • Step 7: Save the default route into the pending transaction
    • Step 8: Verify pending transaction still exists
    • Step 9: Commit with rollback protection
  • Phase 5: Verify Route and Connectivity
    • Step 10: Check the default route
    • Step 11: Confirm TrueNAS route view
    • Step 12: Confirm runtime gateway matches configuration
    • Step 13: Test external connectivity
  • Phase 6: Finalize and Clean Up
    • Step 14: Confirm the committed changes (checkin)
    • Step 15: Restore original description (optional but recommended)
  • Why This Is the Strongest Repair Path
  • Recommended Immediate Command
  • Script Based Solution

High-Level Overview

The issue: TrueNAS has a gateway configured, but the kernel is missing the default route, causing “Network is unreachable” errors (e.g., when contacting update.ixsystems.com).

The fix: Use TrueNAS’s native interface API to:

  • Create a small, safe interface update.
  • Explicitly attach the configured gateway to the pending transaction.
  • Commit with automatic rollback protection.
  • Verify and finalize.

Phase 1: Pre-Flight Diagnostics

Before changing anything, confirm that TrueNAS recognizes the mismatch and that no stale transaction is blocking us.

Step 1: Check for pending changes

Ensures no previous interface operation is stuck.

midclt call interface.has_pending_changes

Expected: False

Step 2: Check if the default route would be removed

Uses a built-in diagnostic to see if TrueNAS detects the gateway/kernel mismatch.

midclt call interface.default_route_will_be_removed

  • If true: TrueNAS recognizes the issue. Proceed with the repair.
  • If false: The middleware is not detecting the missing route via this path. Stop here and investigate further before modifying the interface.

Phase 2: Confirm Current State

Verify that the gateway is configured but missing from the kernel, and confirm the interface is up.

Step 3: Inspect configuration, interface, and routes

Run the following block as one script. It prints key values in a readable format.

echo "=== CONFIGURATION ==="
midclt call network.configuration.config | python3 -c '
import sys, json
d = json.load(sys.stdin)
print("configured gateway:", repr(d["ipv4gateway"]))
print("runtime gateway:", repr(d["state"]["ipv4gateway"]))
print("DNS1:", repr(d["nameserver1"]))
'

echo
echo "=== INTERFACE ==="
ip -4 addr show dev <INTERFACE NAME>

echo
echo "=== ROUTE ==="
ip -4 route

echo
echo "=== TRUE NAS ROUTES ==="
midclt call route.system_routes | python3 -m json.tool

echo
echo "=== PENDING CHANGES ==="
midclt call interface.has_pending_changes

You should currently see:

configured gateway: '[GATEWAY]'
runtime gateway: ''

And you should not see:

default via [GATEWAY] dev <INTERFACE NAME>

Phase 3: Create a Safe Interface Update

TrueNAS requires an actual interface update before save_default_route can attach the gateway to the pending transaction. We will change only the interface description to avoid affecting networking.

Step 4: Get current interface configuration

Use this to confirm current values (name, IP, MTU, description).

midclt call interface.query '[["name","=","enp32s0"]]' | python3 -m json.tool

Key values should be approximately:

name = <INTERFACE NAME>
ipv4_dhcp= false
ipv6_auto= false
aliases= <SERVER IP>/22
mtu= 1500
description = "<INTERFACE NAME>"

Step 5: Apply a temporary description change

This creates a pending interface transaction without altering IP or routing.

midclt call interface.update "enp32s0" '{"description":"enp32s0-route-repair"}'

Verify that a pending change now exists:

midclt call interface.has_pending_changes

Expected: true

If the existing description is already exactly enp32s0-route-repair, choose a different temporary value.

Phase 4: Inject Gateway and Commit (with Rollback Protection)

Now we attach the configured gateway to the pending transaction and commit it safely.

Step 6: Capture the configured gateway

GATEWAY="$(midclt call network.configuration.config | python3 -c '
import sys, json
print(json.load(sys.stdin)["ipv4gateway"])
')"
echo "GATEWAY=${GATEWAY}"

Confirm it matches your expected gateway, e.g.:

GATEWAY=[GATEWAY]

Step 7: Save the default route into the pending transaction

This is the core step: it tells TrueNAS to include the gateway when the interface changes are applied.

midclt call interface.save_default_route "${GATEWAY}"

Step 8: Verify pending transaction still exists

midclt call interface.has_pending_changes

Expected: true

At this point, the kernel route is still missing. The pending transaction now contains:

database configuration
 │
 ▼
interface.update
 │
 ▼
PENDING interface transaction
 │
 ├── description change
 │
 └── default gateway = [GATEWAY]

Step 9: Commit with rollback protection

This applies the pending changes. If something goes wrong, TrueNAS will automatically roll back.

midclt call interface.commit '{"rollback":true,"checkin_timeout":60}'

Behavior:

  • Applies the pending interface changes.
  • Automatically rolls back if application fails.
  • Waits 60 seconds for confirmation (checkin).

Phase 5: Verify Route and Connectivity

Immediately after commit, confirm the route is restored and external connectivity works.

Step 10: Check the default route

ip -4 route show default

Desired result:

default via [GATEWAY] dev <INTERFACE NAME>

Step 11: Confirm TrueNAS route view

midclt call route.system_routes | python3 -m json.tool

You should see an entry similar to:

{
"network": "0.0.0.0",
"netmask": "0.0.0.0",
"gateway": "[GATEWAY]",
"interface": "<INTERFACE NAME>",
"table_id": 254
}

Step 12: Confirm runtime gateway matches configuration

midclt call network.configuration.config | python3 -c 'import sys, json d = json.load(sys.stdin) print("configured gateway:", repr(d["ipv4gateway"])) print("runtime gateway:", repr(d["state"]["ipv4gateway"]))'

Desired result:

configured gateway: '[GATEWAY]'
runtime gateway: '[GATEWAY]'

This confirms the configuration and kernel states are now aligned.

Step 13: Test external connectivity

Run these before the 60-second checkin timeout expires.

ping -c 4 "${GATEWAY}"
ping -c 4 1.1.1.1
getent hosts update.ixsystems.com
curl -4 -I --connect-timeout 10 https://update.ixsystems.com/

If the default route is correct, the original error:

Cannot connect to host update.ixsystems.com:443
[Network is unreachable]

should no longer appear.

Phase 6: Finalize and Clean Up

Once verification succeeds, confirm the changes and restore the original description.

Step 14: Confirm the committed changes (checkin)

Only run this if the route and connectivity tests pass.

midclt call interface.checkin

Then verify no pending changes remain:

midclt call interface.has_pending_changes

Expected: false

Step 15: Restore original description (optional but recommended)

Perform this as a second, clean transaction.

midclt call interface.update "<INTERFACE NAME>" '{"description":"<INTERFACE NAME>"}'
midclt call interface.commit '{"rollback":true,"checkin_timeout":120}'

Verify:

midclt call interface.query '[["name","=","enp32s0"]]' | python3 -c 'import sys, json d = json.load(sys.stdin)[0] print("description:", d["description"]) print("aliases:", d["aliases"])'

Then finalize:

midclt call interface.checkin

Why This Is the Strongest Repair Path

This procedure:

  • Uses only native TrueNAS APIs (no manual ip route hacks).
  • Preserves existing interface configuration.
  • Explicitly re-attaches the configured gateway via save_default_route.
  • Protects against lockouts with rollback=true and checkin_timeout.
  • Aligns with TrueNAS 25.04 behavior where the default route can be removed if the configured gateway does not match the kernel’s installed gateway.

Recommended Immediate Command

Before doing anything else, run:

midclt call interface.default_route_will_be_removed

  • If true: Proceed with this procedure.
  • If false: Stop before interface.update; the middleware is not recognizing the missing route via the expected mechanism, and further investigation is required.

Script Based Solution

This isn't immediately usable unless you're able to SSH into the TrueNAS server and write the script to a drive in the server, or directly connect a USB drive and copy it onto the server.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# ==========================
# TrueNAS Gateway Repair Script
# ==========================
# Role: Expert Linux/TrueNAS Shell Script
# Purpose: 
#   - Compare configured vs runtime IPv4 gateway
#   - If runtime is blank/null or mismatched, trigger a safe interface transaction
#     to permanently sync the runtime gateway to the configured gateway.
# Usage:
#   1. Replace <INTERFACE_NAME> with your actual interface (e.g., enp32s0)
#   2. Run as root or via sudo in the TrueNAS shell
# ==========================

INTERFACE="<INTERFACE_NAME>"
TEMP_DESC="route-repair-$(date +%s)"
ORIGINAL_DESC=""

# Helper: run midclt and return JSON (suppress noisy stderr)
midclt_json() {
    midclt call "$@" 2>/dev/null | python3 -c "
    import sys, json
    try:
        print(json.dumps(json.load(sys.stdin), indent=2))
    except:
        print('')
    "
}

# Helper: extract a nested field from JSON using dot notation
get_field() {
    local json_data="$1"
    local field="$2"
    echo "$json_data" | python3 -c "
    import sys, json
    try:
        data = json.load(sys.stdin)
        keys = '$field'.split('.')
        val = data
        for k in keys:
            if isinstance(val, dict):
                val = val.get(k)
            else:
                val = None
                break
        print(val if val is not None else '')
    except:
        print('')
    "
}

echo "=== TrueNAS Gateway Repair Script ==="
echo "Target Interface: $INTERFACE"

# 1. Fetch network configuration
NET_CONFIG_JSON=$(midclt_json network.configuration.config)
CONFIGURED_GW=$(get_field "$NET_CONFIG_JSON" "ipv4gateway")
RUNTIME_GW=$(get_field "$NET_CONFIG_JSON" "state.ipv4gateway")

echo "Configured Gateway: '$CONFIGURED_GW'"
echo "Runtime Gateway:    '$RUNTIME_GW'"

# 2. Compare gateways
if [[ -n "$CONFIGURED_GW" && "$CONFIGURED_GW" == "$RUNTIME_GW" ]]; then
    echo "Gateways match. No repair needed."
    exit 0
fi

if [[ -z "$CONFIGURED_GW" ]]; then
    echo "ERROR: No configured gateway found. Aborting."
    exit 1
fi

echo "Runtime gateway is missing/blank or mismatched. Initiating repair sequence..."

# 3. Diagnostic (informational)
WILL_REMOVE=$(midclt call interface.default_route_will_be_removed 2>/dev/null || echo "false")
echo "default_route_will_be_removed: $WILL_REMOVE"

# 4. Preserve current interface metadata
IFACE_JSON=$(midclt_json interface.query "[[\"name\",\"=\",\"$INTERFACE\"]]")
IFACE_DATA=$(echo "$IFACE_JSON" | python3 -c "
import sys, json
try:
    print(json.dumps(json.load(sys.stdin)[0]))
except:
    print('')
")

if [[ -z "$IFACE_DATA" ]]; then
    echo "ERROR: Could not retrieve configuration for $INTERFACE. Aborting."
    exit 1
fi

ORIGINAL_DESC=$(get_field "$IFACE_DATA" "description")
echo "Original Description: '$ORIGINAL_DESC'"

# 5. Trigger pending changes with a harmless update
echo "Updating interface description to create pending transaction..."
midclt call interface.update "$INTERFACE" "{\"description\":\"$TEMP_DESC\"}"

PENDING=$(midclt call interface.has_pending_changes 2>/dev/null)
if [[ "$PENDING" != "true" ]]; then
    echo "ERROR: interface.update did not create pending changes. Aborting."
    exit 1
fi
echo "Pending changes: $PENDING"

# 6. Inject configured gateway into pending transaction
echo "Saving default route to pending transaction..."
midclt call interface.save_default_route "$CONFIGURED_GW"

# 7. Commit with automatic rollback protection
echo "Committing interface changes (rollback=true, checkin_timeout=60)..."
midclt call interface.commit '{"rollback":true,"checkin_timeout":60}'

# 8. Verify kernel route
echo "Verifying default route..."
sleep 2
ROUTE_OUTPUT=$(ip -4 route show default 2>/dev/null || true)
if ! echo "$ROUTE_OUTPUT" | grep -q "via $CONFIGURED_GW dev $INTERFACE"; then
    echo "WARNING: Default route not found immediately. Dumping system routes for inspection:"
    midclt call route.system_routes | python3 -m json.tool
else
    echo "Default route confirmed: $ROUTE_OUTPUT"
fi

# 9. Confirm changes (cancel rollback)
echo "Confirming changes (checkin)..."
midclt call interface.checkin

# 10. Restore original description (second transaction)
echo "Restoring original description..."
midclt call interface.update "$INTERFACE" "{\"description\":\"$ORIGINAL_DESC\"}"
midclt call interface.commit '{"rollback":true,"checkin_timeout":60}'
midclt call interface.checkin

# 11. Final verification
echo "=== Final Verification ==="
FINAL_NET_JSON=$(midclt_json network.configuration.config)
FINAL_CONFIG_GW=$(get_field "$FINAL_NET_JSON" "ipv4gateway")
FINAL_RUNTIME_GW=$(get_field "$FINAL_NET_JSON" "state.ipv4gateway")

echo "Configured Gateway: '$FINAL_CONFIG_GW'"
echo "Runtime Gateway:    '$FINAL_RUNTIME_GW'"

if [[ "$FINAL_CONFIG_GW" == "$FINAL_RUNTIME_GW" && -n "$FINAL_RUNTIME_GW" ]]; then
    echo "SUCCESS: Runtime gateway now matches configured gateway."
    exit 0
else
    echo "FAILURE: Gateways still do not match. Manual intervention required."
    exit 1
fi

entry.title: Quick Thoughts: TrueNAS RTL8127 Driver Install Tutorial
entry.summary: While tinkering with my TrueNAS server, I ran into a problem that might be worth sharing with the rest of…
entry.content:
While tinkering with my TrueNAS server, I ran into a problem that might be worth sharing with the rest of you. It relates to installing RTL8127 drivers on versions 24.10+, but before 26.04, which integrates the driver into the OS. TrueNAS 26.04 is very much a beta OS release at the moment, so if you're looking to update an existing TrueNAS server, you might need the help.

Table of Contents

  • What is RTL8127?
  • What You Need
  • Step 0: Install the Card
  • Step 1: Enable Console
  • Step 2: Figure Out Where to Place the Files
  • Step 3: TrueNAS Shell
  • Step 4: Make the Script Executable
  • Step 5: Run the Script
  • Step 6: Watch for Errors
    • Permission denied
    • Script not found
    • Source files not found
    • Build failed
  • Step 7: Copy the Driver
  • Step 8: Make the Driver Persistent
  • Step 9: Update Your Network Settings
  • Updates

What is RTL8127?

RTL8127 is a chip made by Realtek that runs 10 gig ethernet network interface cards. In particular, it's used by a number of cards that use PCI-E x4 (the shortest slot) connectors, which are perfect for slapping into systems that reusing old gaming motherboards.

You can find these cards for $35-70 in July 2026, which is a pretty good price, all things considered.

The downside of this chip is that it's not supported by TrueNAS's built-in drivers, so you can't just plug them into a PCI-E x4 slot and get up and running. There's a bit of work that needs to be done, but luckily, there's a GitHub script for that.

Unluckily, despite being made with AI, the person who made it didn't think to make a tutorial.

So here's mine.

What You Need

  • TrueNAS 24.10+, pre-26.04.
  • RTL8127 network interface card.
  • TrueNAS RTL8127 driver build script
  • Realtek drivers

Always run a scan on the script and driver source code before proceeding with this process.

Step 0: Install the Card

You can install the RTL8127 card before compiling the driver. However, it will not show up as an interface in TrueNAS' web GUI until the process is complete.

Step 1: Enable Console

Once your RTL8127 has arrived, the first thing you should do is go to TrueNAS System > Advanced Settings:

You're going to need to have the text console enabled, which is something you might have disabled.

Click Configure on the Console block, click through the warning about changing settings, and you'll see this:

As the red arrow indicates, you'll want to click Show Text Console without Password Prompt. If you have a monitor and keyboard connected to the server, this setting allows you to change settings without having to log-in. This setting should be disabled for security, but we'll need it later.

Click Save.

Step 2: Figure Out Where to Place the Files

Next, you'll need to figure out where to put all the files. In TrueNAS, your file locations will be something like /mnt/tank/drivers/r8127, /mnt/ssd-storage/r8127, /mnt/[DRIVE]/Apps/Filebrowser.

If you have the File Browser app on your NAS, I highly encourage the use of a File Browser folder, since you may have to redo this process if there's a TrueNAS update.

Since I don't know where you will put it, I'll use [PLACEHOLDER-MOUNT].

After you extract the RTL8127 driver files from the .tar.bz2 file they come in, you should set up the folder like this:

[PLACEHOLDER-MOUNT]
├── truenas_build_r8127_driver.sh
├── r8127-<version>/
│   ├── src/
│   ├── Makefile
│   └── ...

Step 3: TrueNAS Shell

Get into the shell command line interface (CLI) by:

  • System → Shell from the TrueNAS web interface
  • SSH
  • Text Console

You'll then use the cd command to navigate to where the script is:

cd [PLACEHOLDER-MOUNT]

Step 4: Make the Script Executable

You'll need to give the script permissions to execute with the following command:

chmod +x truenas_build_r8127_driver.sh

Verify with the following command, which should show the executable permissions (x):

ls -l truenas_build_r8127_driver.sh

Step 5: Run the Script

Use sudo to execute the script:

sudo ./truenas_build_r8127_driver.sh

Depending on the script, it may:

  • verify the TrueNAS version
  • install required build tools
  • compile the driver
  • build a kernel module
  • install the module
  • update module dependencies

Compilation may take several minutes. All of this takes place in a Docker container, which is why the 

Step 6: Watch for Errors

Monitor the terminal for messages. If the script reports an error, note:

  • the exact error message
  • the command that failed
  • any missing dependency
  • any compiler error

You'll need the error messages for troubleshooting.

Some common issues you might face:

Permission denied

If you receive Permission denied:

Run: chmod +x truenas_build_r8127_driver.sh

Script not found

Verify your current directory: pwd

List files: ls -aux

You should be in the same folder as the build script before trying to initiate it.

Source files not found

Confirm that the driver source exists under [PLACEHOLDER-MOUNT] with: ls -aux

The script can't build the driver if the source files are missing or stored in a different location.

Build failed

Possible causes include:

  • incompatible TrueNAS version
  • missing compiler tools
  • missing kernel headers
  • incorrect driver version
  • unsupported kernel changes

Review the compilation output to identify the first reported error.

Step 7: Copy the Driver

Go to the [PLACEHOLDER-MOUNT] to see the folder generated by Docker during the build process:

Go into the r8127_build folder until you reach the rtl8127 subfolder. Scroll down until you find the r8127.ko file:

Copy this file to the main folder containing the build script.

Once that's done, you can delete the build folder.

Step 8: Make the Driver Persistent

At this point, rebooting the system will deactivate the driver. Now that it's copied, go to System Settings -> Advanced -> Init/Shutdown Scripts.

Click Add, which brings up this interface:

Configure the script with the following settings:

  • Type: Command
  • Command: insmod [PLACEHOLDER-MOUNT]/r8127.ko
  • When: Post Init
  • Enabled: Checked

Click Save to complete the script.

At this point, it is safe to shutdown the server to install the hardware, or reboot to bring up the Text Console.

Step 9: Update Your Network Settings

Now that your driver is being persistently loaded, it's time to change the network settings via the Text Console:

This allows you to remove the settings from the original interface and apply them to the new interface.

If you do not need to copy the settings over, you can simply configure your new interface through the web GUI.

Updates

When a newer driver or OS version is released:

  1. Download the updated source files.
  2. Replace the old source directory.
  3. Run the build script again.
  4. Replace the copied driver with the newest version.
  5. Reboot.

As noted in the script:

This script must be re-run after every TrueNAS SCALE version update to recompile the driver against the new kernel headers.

This process may require the Text Console to execute.

entry.content:
I wasn't planning on doing a major update to this series for a while, partly due to being busy with working on CCNA certifications. But also due to the general hardware price nightmare of 2026 and OPNSense's general jankiness with its API in version 26 making the automation part of project a bit more suspect.

But when you've got major problems, it's time for a major update.

Table of Contents

  • The Context
  • The First Problem
  • The Second Problem
  • ChatGPT Actually Helped
  • Working with Qwen3.6-Uncensored-NEO-CODE
  • Enter OpenCode
  • Configuring OPNSense 26.7
  • How Spectrum Handles DHCP
  • Suricata Configuration
  • Future Upgrade Planning
  • Next Steps
  • Takeaways

The Context

For the first half of the year, things were stable with the older version of the setup file I had created for the wpa_supplicant, which controls the WiFi interface I use to manage OPNSense on the miniPC it runs off of.

OPNSense versions 26.1+ provided no real issues aside from the need to reapply the script whenever an update occurred, because the update would revert the wpa_supplicant file back to its old state.

OPNSense announced a planned upgrade to version 26.7 on July 15, 2026, at which time support for 26.1+ would cease. I waited a few days, checked the r/OPNSense thread on the update, saw that N100 miniPCs like mine had few issues, and proceeded with the update.

The First Problem

After the minor hassle of updating to 26.1.11 to get to update to 26.7, the first real indication of a problem was when I tried to get into the shell to look at wpa_supplicant, and this happened:

The above screenshot is a small segment of the fast moving stream of text that would fill the screen before the miniPC crashed.

What was interesting about this crash was OPNSense would boot properly, allow me to enter the shell, and then crash after about 1-2 minutes from boot completion.

I explored several avenues to dealing with this, including reinstalling OPNSense. I couldn't get the installer to work, so I was left with using an option I had never used before: Reset to Default Configuration.

Since I had a backup of the configuration made before the update, I saw little risk in using this option. And it worked.

The Second Problem

The fact that resetting to default configuration solved the problem at all indicated that it was at least partially due to configuration settings, which promised headaches in the future.

However, the new problem was that I would have to figure what to do with the wpa_supplicant, because resetting to default hadn't enabled it to connect to my home network.

Unfortunately, I managed to botch taking a picture of the actual code for the default wpa_supplicant implementation, so I don't have that as a reference. Even more annoying, the source code is not easily discoverable online, so I was not able to reference that instead.

Attempting to use the old script didn't work, so I was left an option I very much did not like: using ChatGPT to generate diagnostic scripts.

If you've read previous posts in this series, you might be wondering why I would say that. And the answer is very simple: since the start of 2026, the functionality of the free ChatGPT account has steadily degraded (aka enshittification). As of July 2026, if you upload too many documents, you get a cooldown before you can upload more. If you want it to do code, it can't be too big, or it won't show up in the chat window and it can't be compiled into a file you can download. If you use too many token, you get a cooldown on the default model and forced to use a worse model or wait. And so.

ChatGPT Actually Helped

The reason I picked ChatGPT over my local models was because I wasn't sure how context was required to produce a useful script - or even if Qwen 3.6 had useful knowledge on FreeBSD shell coding.

So I was taking a huge chance when I provided ChatGPT this prompt:

role: freebsd shell script expert | context:
- FreeBSD 15+
- WiFi handling change
- WiFi no long connecting
- output target: `/usr/local/scripts/`
- keep filename short for easy copying | task:
- generate script diagnosing wifi stack (firmware, settings, etc...)
- dump data to `.log` file for analysis

This generated the following script:

#!/bin/sh

##############################################################################
# FreeBSD WiFi Diagnostic Script
#
# Output:
#   /tmp/wdiag-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.log
#
##############################################################################

PATH=/bin:/sbin:/usr/bin:/usr/sbin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/local/sbin

if [ "$(id -u)" != "0" ]; then
    echo "Run as root."
    exit 1
fi

TS=$(date +"%Y%m%d-%H%M%S")
LOG="/tmp/wdiag-${TS}.log"

exec >"$LOG" 2>&1

echo "============================================================="
echo "FreeBSD WiFi Diagnostic"
echo "Started: $(date)"
echo "============================================================="
echo

##############################################################################
section()
{
    echo
    echo "============================================================="
    echo "$1"
    echo "============================================================="
}

run()
{
    echo
    echo ">>> $*"
    "$@"
}

##############################################################################

section "SYSTEM"

run uname -a
run freebsd-version
run hostname
run uptime

##############################################################################

section "PCI DEVICES"

run pciconf -lv

##############################################################################

section "USB DEVICES"

if command -v usbconfig >/dev/null 2>&1
then
    run usbconfig
fi

##############################################################################

section "LOADED KERNEL MODULES"

run kldstat

##############################################################################

section "DEVMATCH"

if command -v devmatch >/dev/null 2>&1
then
    run devmatch
fi

##############################################################################

section "INSTALLED FIRMWARE PACKAGES"

pkg info | grep -Ei 'firmware|iwlwifi|rtw88|rtw89|mediatek|ath|wifi|wireless'

##############################################################################

section "WIRELESS INTERFACES"

IFACES=$(ifconfig -l)

for i in $IFACES
do
    if ifconfig "$i" | grep -qi "IEEE"
    then
        echo
        echo "Wireless interface: $i"
    fi
done

##############################################################################

section "IFCONFIG -A"

run ifconfig -a

##############################################################################

section "WIRELESS STATUS"

for i in $(ifconfig -l)
do
    if ifconfig "$i" | grep -qi "IEEE"
    then
        echo
        echo "Interface: $i"

        ifconfig "$i"

        echo
        ifconfig "$i" list scan >/dev/null 2>&1

        echo
        ifconfig "$i" scan
    fi
done

##############################################################################

section "ROUTING"

run netstat -rn

##############################################################################

section "DNS"

cat /etc/resolv.conf

##############################################################################

section "RUNNING NETWORK PROCESSES"

ps axww | grep -E 'wpa|dhclient|netif|routing' | grep -v grep

##############################################################################

section "SERVICE STATUS"

service netif status
service routing status

##############################################################################

section "WPA_SUPPLICANT VERSION"

if command -v wpa_supplicant >/dev/null 2>&1
then
    wpa_supplicant -v
fi

##############################################################################

section "WPA CONFIG"

for f in \
    /etc/wpa_supplicant.conf \
    /etc/wpa_supplicant-*.conf
do
    if [ -f "$f" ]
    then
        echo
        echo "----- $f -----"
        cat "$f"
    fi
done

##############################################################################

section "RC.CONF"

if [ -f /etc/rc.conf ]
then
    cat /etc/rc.conf
fi

##############################################################################

section "LOADER.CONF"

if [ -f /boot/loader.conf ]
then
    cat /boot/loader.conf
fi

##############################################################################

section "LOADER.CONF.LOCAL"

if [ -f /boot/loader.conf.local ]
then
    cat /boot/loader.conf.local
fi

##############################################################################

section "SYSCTL (WIRELESS)"

sysctl -a | grep -Ei \
'80211|wlan|wifi|iwl|rtw|ath|net.wlan'

##############################################################################

section "WLANDEBUG"

if command -v wlandebug >/dev/null 2>&1
then
    wlandebug
fi

##############################################################################

section "DHCLIENT LEASES"

find /var/db -name "dhclient*.leases" -exec sh -c '
for f
do
    echo
    echo "----- $f -----"
    cat "$f"
done
' sh {} +

##############################################################################

section "FIRMWARE DIRECTORIES"

for d in \
    /usr/local/share/firmware \
    /boot/firmware \
    /lib/firmware
do
    if [ -d "$d" ]
    then
        echo
        echo "$d"
        ls -laR "$d"
    fi
done

##############################################################################

section "DMESG (WIRELESS)"

dmesg | grep -Ei \
'iwl|iwx|iwm|ath|rtw|rtwn|urtw|run|ral|rum|otus|rsu|wifi|wlan|firmware|80211'

##############################################################################

section "LAST 500 DMESG LINES"

dmesg | tail -500

##############################################################################

section "BOOT MESSAGES"

if [ -f /var/run/dmesg.boot ]
then
    cat /var/run/dmesg.boot
fi

##############################################################################

section "PKG INFO"

pkg info

##############################################################################

section "PACKAGE VERSIONS"

pkg info | grep -Ei \
'wpa|supplicant|firmware|drm|wifi|wireless'

##############################################################################

section "NETWORK CONFIG FILES"

for f in \
    /etc/hosts \
    /etc/resolv.conf
do
    if [ -f "$f" ]
    then
        echo
        echo "----- $f -----"
        cat "$f"
    fi
done

##############################################################################

section "END"

echo
echo "Completed: $(date)"
echo
echo "Diagnostic log:"
echo "$LOG"

I transferred the script to the MiniPC on a USB, and executed it. Uploading the generated log to ChatGPT provided this analysis:

Based on the diagnostic log, the Wi-Fi hardware and firmware are functioning correctly. The failure occurs later in the initialization process.

## Primary root cause

The most significant error is:

```text
ifconfig: interface wlan0 already exists
/etc/rc.d/wpa_supplicant: ERROR: Failed to create wlan0
```

This indicates that the system is attempting to create the cloned `wlan0` interface even though it already exists.

This is **not** a firmware failure or a driver crash.

Instead, it points to one of:

* duplicate interface creation
* duplicate network initialization
* OPNsense startup scripts conflicting with FreeBSD rc scripts
* stale interface configuration after migration to the new `iwlwifi` driver

---

## Evidence

### 1. Driver loads successfully

The Intel AX101 is detected correctly.

```text
Detected Intel(R) Wi-Fi 6 AX101
successfully loaded firmware image
loaded firmware version ...
```

No firmware errors appear.

---

### 2. Firmware is present

The correct firmware exists:

```
iwlwifi-so-a0-hr-b0-89.ucode
```

---

### 3. Hardware initializes

The interface obtains a MAC address:

```
base HW address:
Ethernet address:
```

This means

* PCI
* DMA
* firmware upload
* RF initialization

all completed successfully.

---

### 4. The interface already exists

Later the log reports

```
Wireless interface:
iwlwifi0_wlan0
```

which means the clone **already exists**.

Yet rc later attempts

```
create wlan0
```

again.

That fails.

---

## 5. No association attempt

I do **not** see any of:

* authentication
* association
* RSN negotiation
* WPA handshake
* scan failures

There are no messages like

```
Associated
AUTH
DEAUTH
4-way handshake
SSID
```

That means Wi-Fi never reached the stage of talking to the AP.

---

## 6. No DHCP attempt

The DHCP lease section is empty.

This is expected because there was never a usable wireless interface.

---

# Things that are NOT the problem

### Firmware

Firmware loads correctly.

---

### Unsupported chipset

The card is fully recognized.

```
Intel Wi-Fi 6 AX101
```

---

### Missing kernel module

The module is loaded.

```
if_iwlwifi.ko
```

---

### Missing firmware package

Firmware exists.

---

### RF kill

```
RFIm is deactivated, reason = 4
```

This message is common for Intel LinuxKPI drivers and is **not** itself an indication that the radio is disabled. The device proceeds to initialize and receives its MAC address afterward. 

---

# What I suspect

Given the log, my confidence ranking is:

## Problems in the current script

### 1. Incorrect interface creation

The script currently does

```sh
ifconfig "${wpa_supplicant_parent}" create \
    wlandev "${wpa_supplicant_parent}"
```

For Intel this expands to

```sh
ifconfig iwlwifi0 create wlandev iwlwifi0
```

This is **no longer reliable** on newer kernels.

The supported form is

```sh
ifconfig wlan create wlandev iwlwifi0 name iwlwifi0_wlan0
```

or

```sh
ifconfig wlan0 create wlandev iwlwifi0
```

depending on configuration.

Using the parent interface as the object being created now returns

```
SIOCIFCREATE2
Invalid argument
```

---

### 2. Script ignores rc.conf

FreeBSD 15 expects the networking framework to own cloned interfaces.

Instead of manually creating

```
iwlwifi0_wlan0
```

the preferred configuration is

```sh
wlans_iwlwifi0="wlan0"
```

or

```sh
wlans_iwlwifi0="iwlwifi0_wlan0"
```

Then

```
service netif start
```

creates it.

The rc.d script should **verify** the interface exists.

It should **not** normally create it itself.

---

### 3. Wrong REQUIRE dependency

Current:

```sh
REQUIRE: NETWORKING
```

`NETWORKING` completes before cloned wlan interfaces exist.

Instead use

```sh
REQUIRE: netif
AFTER: devd
```

or simply

```
REQUIRE: LOGIN netif
```

depending on when you want it.

Otherwise

```
service wpa_supplicant start
```

runs before wlan creation.

---

### 4. Missing parent validation

Before doing anything the script should verify

```sh
ifconfig -l
```

contains

```
iwlwifi0
```

If not

```

```

is insufficient.

It also needs

```
kldload firmware
```

(or the proper Intel firmware module)

and wait for the device.

---

### 5. Race condition

Immediately after loading

```
if_iwlwifi
```

the firmware loads asynchronously.

The script immediately executes

```
ifconfig wlan create
```

before firmware initialization finishes.

The result is

```
Invalid argument
```

A retry loop is much safer:

```sh
i=0

while [ $i -lt 20 ]
do
    if ifconfig iwlwifi0 >/dev/null 2>&1
    then
        break
    fi

    sleep 1
    i=$((i+1))
done
```

---

### 6. Wrong configuration filename

The script defines

```sh
wpa_supplicant_conf="/var/etc/wpa_supplicant_wlan0.conf"
```

but generated

```
/var/etc/wpa_supplicant_iwlwifi0_wlan0.conf
```

These do **not** match.

So even if the interface existed,

```
wpa_supplicant
```

would fail because the configuration file does not exist.

---

### 7. No interface existence check

Before starting

```
wpa_supplicant
```

the script should verify

```sh
ifconfig "${iface}"
```

returns success.

If not

```
err 1 "${iface} does not exist"
```

instead of attempting to launch.

---

### 8. Missing carrier wait

Even after the interface exists,

```
802.11
```

is not immediately ready.

Wait until

```
ifconfig wlan0
```

reports

```
status: no carrier
```

or

```
status: associated
```

before launching `wpa_supplicant`.

The service should follow this sequence:

```
Load firmware
        ↓
Load if_iwlwifi
        ↓
Wait for iwlwifi0
        ↓
Verify parent exists
        ↓
Verify wlan clone exists
        ↓
Create clone only if missing
        ↓
Bring interface down
        ↓
Bring interface up
        ↓
Wait for 802.11 initialization
        ↓
Launch wpa_supplicant
        ↓

        ↓
Run DHCP
```
